# UI/UX design: research methods
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/ui-ux-design-research-methods/

# UI/UX design: research methods — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for UI/UX design: research methods. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.4.1 · generated 2026-11-09 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## Definitions

- [statement] User needs are one framing input alongside organizational and wider-system constraints. GOV.UK includes policy intent and operational constraints; Joffres argues that good design moves between user, strategic, planetary and societal needs. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://marvelapp.com/blog/design-thinking-isnt-the-problem-human-centered-design/
- [statement] SUS is an overall post-test perceived-usability questionnaire; SEQ is a post-task rating of the difficulty of the task just attempted. Choose the instrument according to the level of experience being evaluated. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://measuringu.com/papers/Sauro_Dumas_CHI2009.pdf
- [statement] Treat method maps as adaptable guidance: classifications are not rigid, and research questions, organizational resources, and stakeholder needs shape the approach. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/which-ux-research-methods/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.userinterviews.com/ux-research-field-guide-chapter/how-to-choose-a-research-method

## Structure and components

- [statement] GOV.UK recommends turning research questions into ordered interview topics, starter questions, and possible follow-ups; pilot the structure with a colleague and revise unclear questions or awkward flow before creating the discussion guide. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/critical-incident-technique/
- [statement] A tree test isolates category structure and text labels from visual layout and other contextual cues. Its results do not by themselves establish findability in the fully designed site, where design and search can change behavior. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://measuringu.com/tree-testing-ia/, https://raw.studio/blog/card-sorting-and-tree-testing, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-tree-test-results/
- [statement] Card-sort groupings and participant-created names are design inputs, not a ready-made navigation structure: researchers must interpret them and evaluate candidate hierarchies. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-definition/, https://www.uxmatters.com/mt/archives/2007/09/card-sorting-mistakes-made-and-lessons-learned.php
- [statement] SUS contains 10 items with five response options. Its transformed score ranges from 0 to 100 and is not a percentage or a percentile rank. (medium confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/

## How it works

- [statement] Balance clarification against interference: silent observation preserves more of the activity’s natural flow but can leave its meaning unclear; occasional questions add understanding, while step-by-step explanation changes how people perform the activity. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Observation may miss rare events because its time window is limited; a critical-incident interview can elicit unusual events outside that window, with the memory and typicality limitations stated above. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/critical-incident-technique/
- [statement] NN/G recommends explicitly transitioning from the introductory interview to watching actual work; agree that the participant can defer interruptions and redirect summaries or grievance lists back to normal work when needed. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Ask for clarification when an observed action is unclear and let participants correct interpretations; reserve final questions for the end so understanding can improve without repeatedly interrupting work. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] A process diagram alone is insufficient preparation for complex framing work. Joffres calls design processes scaffolding and emphasizes practitioner abilities; van der Bijl-Brouwer concludes that framing complex societal problems requires a sophisticated skillset and expertise. (medium confidence) — https://marvelapp.com/blog/design-thinking-isnt-the-problem-human-centered-design/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405872618301114
- [statement] NN/G cautions that predefined categories in hybrid sorts can bias participants toward similarly structured categories; it prefers tree testing over closed sorting when the goal is evaluating navigation categories. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-definition/
- [statement] Practitioner experience warns against treating every findability problem as a taxonomy problem: navigation controls and search quality may need attention even when card sorting is available. (medium confidence) — https://www.uxmatters.com/mt/archives/2007/09/card-sorting-mistakes-made-and-lessons-learned.php · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://measuringu.com/tree-testing-ia/
- [statement] Pilot the tasks and instructions before launch. Unmoderated instructions must stand alone because no facilitator is present to clarify misunderstandings during the session. (high confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/
- [statement] Unmoderated prototypes need enough scenario context to make the task understandable without an interview. David Hamill warns about missing backstory; Elise Nguyen separately reports needing more prototype context when she could not interview participants directly. (medium confidence) — https://david-hamill.medium.com/unmoderated-usability-testing-some-mistakes-to-avoid-8f2d1a3d5732 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://elisenguyen.com/work/mongodb-billing
- [statement] Recruit participants who match the target users. Plan accessibility support, and let assistive-technology users use their own devices where feasible because personal configurations can be hard to replicate. (high confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/
- [statement] Choose moderated sessions when clarification and probing are important; unmoderated remote sessions suit focused tasks and flexible parallel scheduling, but lack live action-specific follow-up and may yield unusable sessions if participants misunderstand tasks or encounter technical trouble. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/
- [statement] Do not force substantially different observed journeys into one map. GOV.UK recommends a consolidated map when participants share stages and similar steps, and separate maps when groups have significantly different stages and steps. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/creating-an-experience-map
- [statement] Frog recommends testing a proposed service through prototypes before implementation so that risky assumptions encounter real users and real-world conditions. (low confidence) — https://www.frog.co/designmind/intentional-healthcare-delivery-with-service-design
- [statement] A diagram should support investigation and change: blueprint dependencies can expose service weaknesses and redundant work. Nielsen Norman Group recommends prototyping future process changes before implementation and tracking changes against service goals. These are recommended uses, not proof that producing a diagram alone improves outcomes. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprinting-faq/
- [statement] SEQ asks about perceived task difficulty immediately after each task, whereas SUS concerns the overall session; use the task-level question to compare tasks, keeping tasks comparable when benchmarking. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://measuringu.com/papers/Sauro_Dumas_CHI2009.pdf
- [statement] UMUX-LITE uses two positively worded items about capabilities meeting requirements and ease of use. Its original researchers reported concurrent validity with SUS in two surveys and proposed it as a shorter alternative when a longer questionnaire is undesirable. (medium confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2470654.2481287 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://measuringu.com/umux-lite/
- [statement] Treat validation as evidence for a particular instrument and context. The Greek UMUX-LITE study found good reliability and concurrent validity on the websites it studied, while explicitly limiting generalization because it tested only two systems of the same type. (low confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3635059.3635075
- [statement] UMUX-Lite asks whether the system’s capabilities meet the respondent’s requirements and whether the system is easy to use. Its two positive items cover perceived usefulness and ease of use; it is a shorter alternative when questionnaire burden matters. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/umux-lite/

## How-to and procedures

- [statement] Use task paths to decide whether to rename, regroup, or provide multiple routes to content. ONRR’s tree test exposed competing category expectations and led the team to propose cross-listing resources and reorganizing categories. (low confidence) — https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing
- [statement] Prefer moderation when understanding an unexpected action requires clarification or follow-up. Unmoderated remote studies suit focused questions with self-contained tasks and can run on participants’ own schedules. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://github.com/sourcegraph/handbook/blob/main/content/departments/product/design/research/usability-testing-how-to.md
- [statement] Use personas to express behavior, needs, goals and relevant context. Use jobs-to-be-done to express the outcome sought and the situation and motivations behind it; demographic attributes alone do not explain the job. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/personas-jobs-be-done/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.intercom.com/blog/using-job-stories-design-features-ui-ux

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] If work cannot safely be interrupted, observe with minimal interference and defer clarification questions until an appropriate stopping point or after the session. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Define the accepted destinations for each tree-test task before interpreting success. Success counts participants who select a correct final location; visiting it and then choosing another location is failure. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tree-testing/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-tree-test-results/
- [statement] In ONRR’s card-sort case, a small sample spread across two audiences left some cards without a strong placement pattern; this is a case-specific sample limitation, not a universal participant threshold. (low confidence) — https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing
- [statement] Limit task-learning effects: ONRR observed participants learning tree categories quickly and emphasized fewer tasks and randomized order; NN/G recommends assigning each participant only one tree version when comparing trees. (medium confidence) — https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tree-testing/
- [statement] Think-aloud asks participants to verbalize thoughts during tasks, providing context beyond observable actions. In remote unmoderated testing, researchers cannot remind a quiet participant to continue speaking as they can in a moderated session. (high confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/
- [statement] Do not use a satisfaction score alone to diagnose an interface failure or assume that a favorable SUS score proves successful task performance. Combine ratings with observed performance and investigation of the problems. (medium confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/measuring-perceived-usability/
- [statement] Use Goals–Signals–Metrics to make measurement actionable: articulate the product or feature goal, identify behavior or attitudes that signal success or failure, then define specific metrics. The official publication describes the framework as a way to connect product goals and metrics. (medium confidence) — https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/36299.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/
- [statement] Small samples limit inference even when an instrument is reliable. Sauro recommends a confidence interval around the sample SUS score because small samples produce imprecise population estimates; Sauro and Dumas found low detection rates for post-task instruments at small sample sizes in their experiment. (medium confidence) — https://measuringu.com/sus/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://measuringu.com/papers/Sauro_Dumas_CHI2009.pdf
- [statement] The Goals–Signals–Metrics process starts with a product or feature goal, identifies behavioral or attitudinal signals of success or failure, and translates them into metrics. Prefer signals specific to the goal, normalize raw counts when user-base growth would distort interpretation, and check logging coverage and automated traffic. (low confidence) — https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/36299.pdf
- [statement] Scale research effort to the risk, consequences, and reversibility of the decision as well as research cost; expensive choices justify stronger triangulation than simple, easily reversible choices. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/triangulation-better-research-results-using-multiple-ux-methods/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://enterprisearchitecture.harvard.edu/user-research-methods-and-recommendations
- [statement] Treat generated persona content as a representation requiring validation, not as observed human evidence: the conceptual analysis of generative personas describes convincing fabricated content as a hallucination risk, while NN/G requires persona characteristics to be grounded in real-user research. (medium confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1071581925002149 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/persona/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Use open, neutral questions and short clarification probes; ask for concrete past episodes instead of inviting agreement with a proposed product or predicting future use. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
- [statement] Discovery interviews investigate users’ circumstances, problems, and existing ways of addressing them; use the conversation to understand their world rather than pitch a proposed product. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
- [statement] Use open, neutral starter questions and short probes for detail; ask participants to explain actions or clarify meaning rather than supply an expected answer. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Ground interviews in specific stories and real examples; asking about the last occurrence, what the person did, and what they previously tried keeps discovery focused on reported past behavior rather than hypothetical product adoption. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
- [statement] NN/G cautions that retrospective process accounts can omit important reasoning and habitual details, and recommends validating recollections with observation; a past-behavior account should therefore be treated as a report to investigate rather than guaranteed truth. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] NN/G advises using direct observation with later clarification when participants cannot safely be interrupted, and scopes contextual inquiry toward understanding complex work rather than assuming its interview component is always necessary. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Treat lifecycle phases as revisitable activities rather than a one-way approval sequence: the Design Council says learning can return teams to earlier work, and van der Bijl-Brouwer’s public and social innovation study found nonlinear co-evolution of problem frames and solution spaces. (medium confidence) — https://www.designcouncil.org.uk/our-resources/the-double-diamond/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405872618301114
- [statement] In their survey of practitioners’ client innovation projects, Dell’Era and colleagues report that reframing practices were positively associated with innovation radicalness whereas framing practices were not. They explicitly state that their cross-sectional data limit causal inference over time; this is contextual evidence rather than proof that a lifecycle guarantees innovation. (low confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0148296326002559
- [statement] Human-centered design starts from understanding the people affected by a problem; IDEO U describes involving stakeholders throughout the process rather than only at its beginning or end. (medium confidence) — https://www.designcouncil.org.uk/our-resources/the-double-diamond/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.ideou.com/blogs/inspiration/what-is-human-centered-design?srsltid=AYCX9vKFS7wpqGtEIHQ-ADifYB5mUqj0FGMs5ntRc0yv06O8XicRYcJ8
- [statement] For assumptions, GOV.UK distinguishes hard constraints from processes that can change and uses constraints to prioritize risky assumptions for alpha. IDEO U likewise advises remaining receptive to being wrong rather than treating assumptions as settled knowledge. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.ideou.com/blogs/inspiration/what-is-human-centered-design?srsltid=AYCX9vKFS7wpqGtEIHQ-ADifYB5mUqj0FGMs5ntRc0yv06O8XicRYcJ8
- [statement] Treat card-sort patterns as input to a draft taxonomy, then evaluate its labels and hierarchy through tree testing and revise problematic branches. Sorting results require design judgment rather than automatic adoption as the final structure. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://raw.studio/blog/card-sorting-and-tree-testing
- [statement] Use divergent navigation paths to consider cross-listing rather than forcing every item into one location. ONRR proposed cross-listing resources after participants split between plausible categories; NN/G recommends using observed demand rather than adding every theoretically possible placement. (medium confidence) — https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interpreting-tree-test-results/
- [statement] Use representative content and clear card labels, and examine audience differences rather than assuming all users organize information alike. In the ONRR case, researchers selected cards using usage and search data, analyzed audiences separately, and found unclear labels impeded sorting. (low confidence) — https://digital.gov/2022/01/06/open-source-information-architecture-design-using-the-tools-you-have-to-conduct-card-sorting-and-tree-testing
- [statement] Pilot card labels and avoid repeated wording that encourages superficial word matching instead of meaningful grouping. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-definition/
- [statement] Recruit actual or likely users of the service. Use screening questions about relevant circumstances or behavior rather than relying only on panel demographics. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://david-hamill.medium.com/unmoderated-usability-testing-some-mistakes-to-avoid-8f2d1a3d5732
- [statement] In its research on remote unmoderated think-aloud testing, MeasuringU reports a tradeoff: verbalizations can clarify behavior and aid problem discovery, while thinking aloud can increase task time and dropout. Its authors advise choosing according to the study objective rather than assuming think-aloud is always preferable. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/ta-summary-2023/
- [statement] Remote testing can reach geographically dispersed users and show behavior on their own computers, while introducing technical troubleshooting demands; remote versus in-person location is a separate choice from whether a facilitator moderates the session. (high confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/remote-usability-tests/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Discovery interviews explore users’ circumstances, needs and problems; contextual inquiry combines interviewing with observation while people work in their usual environment. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Keep discovery conversations centered on actual problems, actions and workarounds. Pitching a solution or asking whether someone would use it risks polite agreement being mistaken for evidence. (medium confidence) — https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews
- [statement] Contextual inquiry combines observing real activities in the user’s normal environment with questions about how and why the work happens; contextual observation can expose effects of equipment, documents, and distractions. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Concrete examples still depend on memory: recalled accounts may lose details, and critical-incident interviews can emphasize extreme events while missing ordinary usage. Do not treat a detailed story as a complete record of behavior. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/critical-incident-technique/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Make the transition from conversation to observation explicit. Explain that the participant should continue normal work, how questions will interrupt it and that they may defer an interruption; otherwise they may stay in interview mode. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry
- [statement] Record observed actions separately from interpretations, then ask participants to clarify what happened and correct your understanding. A wrap-up provides time to check interpretations without repeatedly interrupting the work. (medium confidence) — https://dscout.com/people-nerds/behind-scenes-contextual-inquiry · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Obtain informed consent and explain the session before observation or interviewing; NN/G also calls for confidentiality discussion and approval for recording, while GOV.UK says to reconfirm consent before recording something new. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-in-depth-interviews · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/contextual-research-and-observation, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] Actively seek contrary information and avoid communicating a preferred answer: prior beliefs can shape the interviewer’s interpretation, and participants may supply the answers they think the researcher wants. (medium confidence) — https://www.producttalk.org/glossary-discovery-confirmation-bias/ · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/
- [statement] NYU recommends looking for existing investments of time or money and workarounds as evidence of a problem; this is practitioner guidance for discovery, not a quantified predictive rule. (low confidence) — https://entrepreneur.nyu.edu/blog/2026/03/28/stop-asking-what-they-want-why-customer-discovery-is-about-problems-not-products/
- [statement] The Design Council names its Double Diamond activities Discover, Define, Develop and Deliver: understand the problem, use discovery insights to reframe it, explore alternative answers, and test small-scale solutions to reject or improve them. (low confidence) — https://www.designcouncil.org.uk/our-resources/the-double-diamond/
- [statement] Frame an assigned solution as a problem before committing to it. Interrogate the brief, break down assumptions, and keep the initial problem statement open to revision through contact with people affected by it. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://uxdesign.cc/how-to-properly-frame-your-design-challenge-eccb4d89cb83
- [statement] A useful framing exercise states the intended impact, records context and constraints, and revisits the question as understanding develops; scope also needs an explicit agreement about what falls outside the problem. (medium confidence) — https://uxdesign.cc/how-to-properly-frame-your-design-challenge-eccb4d89cb83 · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works
- [statement] In GOV.UK’s delivery model, discovery ends with a decision whether to enter alpha. The decision considers whether a viable service would help users and whether pursuing it is cost effective; stopping after discovery can be the appropriate outcome. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works
- [statement] GOV.UK recommends identifying hard and soft constraints during discovery. If work continues, dependencies that could make the service unviable should inform which risky assumptions receive attention during alpha. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works
- [statement] GOV.UK’s transition to alpha calls for an understanding of the wider problem context, ideas to test and their initial priority, a rough team plan, and a plan for measuring success. These provide concrete readiness criteria for that transition. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works
- [statement] Problem framing should allow alternatives to building the initially proposed service: GOV.UK explicitly lists content, campaigns, partnerships and better advice as possible responses, while Kal Joffres describes a project whose learning changed its initial app-education brief toward behaviour change. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: research methods · also: https://marvelapp.com/blog/design-thinking-isnt-the-problem-human-centered-design/
- [statement] IDEO U presents Inspiration, Ideation and Implementation as overlapping phases; its account covers learning from people, translating insights into opportunities through early prototypes, and refining concepts with implementation planning. These are IDEO U’s phase labels. (low confidence) — https://www.ideou.com/blogs/inspiration/what-is-human-centered-design?srsltid=AYCX9vKFS7wpqGtEIHQ-ADifYB5mUqj0FGMs5ntRc0yv06O8XicRYcJ8
